Partisan labels were rare in bios, and the identity markers accounts did display in their profiles focused most on their professional roles, content creation, and family and relationships. Political Specialists, the accounts organized around politics, posted the most political content, accounting for 29.1% of political videos in our sample but only 10.1% of their views. Prolific Celebrities and Lifestyle Creators received 86.2% of all views for political videos in our sample. On TikTok, political reach belongs less to political accounts than to those for which politics is occasional, and classifying accounts by political identity or institutional role would miss most of it.

articles.title: Uncovering Hidden Populations: A Network-Based Approach to Estimate Child Trafficking Prevalence
articles.authors: Dennis M. Feehan, Guy Grossman, Biz Herman, Maya Shuen Lu, Cecilia Hyunjung Mo
articles.abstract: Measuring hidden populations, such as child trafficking victims, is difficult: victims are hard to reach and are often reluctant to disclose their experiences, so direct surveys understate prevalence. We evaluate network elicitation as an alternative, comparing estimates based on reports about close friends, about acquaintances, and self-reports. We field all three in a single nationally representative household survey of 1,474 Jamaican children aged 12 to 17, who report on themselves and on their networks, and we measure seven locally common forms of trafficking. Self-reports show that forced hazardous work (3.2 percent) and domestic servitude (2.1 percent) are the most prevalent forms, while forced criminality in gangs (0.4 percent) and commercial sexual exploitation (0.04 percent) are the least prevalent, despite the latter's public discourse prominence. Prevalence estimation based on acquaintance networks, a popular approach to estimating hidden populations, performed poorly, returning estimates falling well below direct estimates. By contrast, reports about close friends, which to our knowledge have not previously been used to estimate trafficking prevalence, adjusted for information transmission rates, yield estimates that are 1.7 to 2.8 times larger than self-reported estimates for six of the seven forms. We conclude that close-friend reports are the more defensible approach: unlike self-reports, they are less affected by reluctance to disclose victimization, and unlike acquaintance reports, they rely on a measurable transmission rate and on respondents' closer knowledge of their friends.

articles.title: Same Job, Different Status? The Social Significance of Network Status Deviation Across 28 Societies
articles.authors: Leo Azzollini, Giacomo Melli, Stefani Scherer
articles.abstract: Social status is a key dimension of stratification. Since Weber, social honor belongs to persons and groups and is expressed partly through the company they keep. Yet occupational status scales assign the same status to everyone in the same job. We introduce Network Status Deviation (NSD): the distance between the weighted mean status of a person’s contacts and that of their occupational peers’ contacts, capturing whether a person keeps better, worse, or similar company than their peers. Leveraging ISSP 2017 position-generator data across 28 societies, we derive this measure from original commensality, ISEI, and SIOPS scores. Net of class, education, and income, NSD and occupational status are jointly associated with subjective social position, health and well-being, social trust, and socio-political participation and orientations, with magnitudes comparable to class and education. To illuminate the social significance of status, the company people keep is as important as their occupation.

articles.title: Exercitus: A Registry of Military Exercises in the Baltic Sea Region, 2015-2026
articles.abstract: Exercitus is a registry of military exercises in the Baltic Sea region from 2015 to 2026. Release 0.5.2 contains 1,658 exercise editions. Each recorded date, location, participant and personnel figure is tied to the words of the source it came from. The organizer's declared personnel count is kept apart from other reported estimates, and the registry records how exercises relate to each other: umbrella exercises and their parts, annual cycles, and exercises held more than once a year. The pipeline combines extraction by a language model with deterministic checks against the source text and with rules and corrections signed by a person. One reviewer checked 401 randomly drawn values from release 0.4.5; 85.5% of the 379 values that could be judged were correct. On a held-out test of extraction from source texts, the model read 91.3% of 126 values correctly. A preliminary completeness check found 20 of 23 reference exercises, a benchmark too small to establish coverage across the full period or region. In our tests, adding tasks to the extraction prompt lowered extraction accuracy, and the model's classifications of exercise kind and structure stayed below the acceptance threshold set in advance. The model therefore extracts values and proposes classifications and relationships, and a person accepts or rejects them through signed rules and corrections. The registry supports the study of reported military exercises and of disagreements between sources. Its limitations include uneven coverage, repeated reporting of the same underlying claims and errors in individual values.

articles.title: Does Longer Comprehensive Schooling Weaken the Association Between Genetic Predisposition and Mental Health? Evidence from Finland
articles.authors: INVEST Flagship, Henrik Dobewall, Aleksi Karhula, Felix C Tropf, Tobias Wolfram, Mika Haapanen, Petri Böckerman, Maria Vaalavuo
articles.abstract: Education is a key socioeconomic determinant of health that may mitigate the effects of genetic predisposition. This study examines whether Finland’s 1970s comprehensive school reform attenuated the association between polygenic scores (PGS) and psychiatric diagnoses and psychotropic medication use in adulthood. Using genetically informed register data for cohorts 1961–1965 (N = 3,936; 54.75% female), we exploit exogenous variation across municipalities and within birth years generated by the reform’s staggered rollout. Across 11 models, none of the overall reform-exposure × PGS interactions reached nominal statistical significance. Among women, one nominally significant interaction suggested that comprehensive schooling might have weakened the association between genetic predisposition to depression and later mental-health diagnoses, but it does not survive correction for multiple testing. However, the study had limited statistical power to detect small G×E interaction effects. We interpret these findings in light of previous studies from Finland, Sweden, the UK, and the US.

articles.title: Türkiye's Value Map: A Current Look at What Society Cares About
articles.abstract: Public debate in Türkiye often assumes that society’s values are changing rapidly, whether toward individualism, conservatism, or a break between generations, yet such claims are rarely tested against representative data. This report describes the value priorities of adults in Türkiye using a nationally representative telephone survey conducted in August–September 2026 (n = 993). Values were measured with a twenty-item scale adapted from the Human Values Scale of the twelfth round of the European Social Survey (ESS) and grounded in Schwartz’s refined theory of basic human values. The findings are compared with ESS measurements of Türkiye from 2004 and 2008, with Turkish value studies dating back to the 1970s, with twenty-nine ESS countries, and with the pan-cultural value hierarchy. Differences are evaluated by effect size rather than statistical significance, and shared values are treated as findings in their own right. Values in Türkiye form a tiered structure rather than a strict rank order. Security, Face, Benevolence, Universalism, and Humility are endorsed with high and closely similar importance, with Security and Face at the top. More than 90% of respondents rate protecting nature, a strong state able to protect its citizens, personal safety, and never being humiliated as very important. Conformity, Self-Direction, Tradition, Hedonism, Stimulation, and Achievement form a second, more selectively endorsed cluster. Within Power, wealth is considered important by two thirds of respondents, while exercising control over others is clearly rejected. This profile is shared across social groups. For the most highly valued values, no difference by age, education, gender, or region exceeds a small effect size. Age is the main dividing line, operating through Tradition, Conformity, and Self-Direction, but these differences reflect the intensity with which the same values are held rather than a generational rupture. The core structure has also been stable over time. Security, Benevolence, Universalism, and Tradition form the top cluster in 2004, 2008, and 2026 alike. Compared with other societies, Türkiye shares the common hierarchy in which Benevolence, Universalism, and Security rank highest. What distinguishes it is the relatively high importance of Tradition and Rule Conformity and the relatively low importance of Self-Direction. Read together with classic analyses of state and society in Türkiye, the findings suggest that expectations of a protective state and an ethic of solidarity rooted in close relationships have broad counterparts at the level of individual values, and they set clear limits on common narratives of value change.

articles.title: Where and how much to invest in bicycle networks: Trip-based cost–benefit optimisation under uncertain uptake
articles.authors: Afshin Jafari, Shuai Zhang, Sapan Tiwari, Ryan Turner
articles.abstract: Choosing where to invest in bicycle infrastructure requires an understanding of the benefits for existing and potential riders, as well as how different projects function together. We used a trip-based model to examine project selection and expenditure for Greater Melbourne’s Strategic Cycling Corridors. The model assesses safety benefits, mode shifts, economic benefits and emission reductions following road infrastructure improvements, and identifies the projects that maximise expected net present value (NPV) within a capital funding limit. Under Reference delivery costs, the model selected 41 projects with capital expenditure of $20.6 million, with expected NPV of $14.9 million and a benefit–cost ratio (BCR) of 1.62. To examine how costs affect investment, we repeated selection under lower and higher rates. Lower costs supported 101 upgrades and 35 new protected sections; reference costs supported 38 upgrades and three new sections; and Higher costs supported six upgrades but no new sections. To test whether accounting for lower uptake changes investment decisions, we tested the model giving greater importance to returns when fewer people change mode. This reduced reference-cost expenditure to $18.7 million while leaving expected NPV almost unchanged. To assess whether joint appraisal changes selection, we compared it with separate project appraisal. In the comparison with the largest gain, joint optimisation selected two additional projects and increased risk-adjusted net value by $0.10 million under Reference costs. Therefore, by demonstrating how delivery costs, route and safety assumptions influence the selected program, we showed the importance of assessing both investment scale and project priorities under uncertain assumptions.

articles.title: Women's Vote during the 2016-2024 US Presidential Elections: Family roles, Employment, and Political Choice
articles.authors: M. Pia Campagna, Shane Poole, Riley Bove
articles.abstract: When do family roles and economic interests shape political choice? Married women outside the labor force have become a reference point in American political discourse since 2016, yet whether they vote differently from married women in paid work, once their backgrounds are considered, has not been examined with contemporary data. Using the Cooperative Election Study for 2016, 2020 and 2024 (15,633 married women aged 25-60, of whom 4,122 identified as homemakers), we estimated the difference in Republican presidential vote between homemakers and employed married women, adjusting for age, race and education and, in supplemental analyses, for family income, children and religion. Homemakers were 5.9 percentage points more likely to vote Republican across the pooled elections after adjustment (3.5 points after further adjustment). The gap was 2.8 points in 2016, 4.9 in 2020 and 10.3 in 2024, and in 2024 it was concentrated almost entirely among mothers, at 11.9 points against 1.1 among women without a child at home. Demographic characteristics fixed before labor-force exit accounted for most of the unadjusted difference and partisanship for the remainder. Three further results bear on this interpretation. First, married men outside the labor force leaned in the opposite direction. Second, homemakers differed from employed wives on gender-role attitudes but not on abortion, moral traditionalism or affect toward the Republican party. Third, longitudinal 2020-2024 data showed negligible vote switching among women already at home. Homemakers were 12 points less likely to be validated voters in 2024 but this was fully accounted for by demographics, and non-voting homemakers were at least as Republican in intention as those who voted. The gap was more closely associated with beliefs about family and gender roles than with economic position. This is notable because policies supporting women's economic security, health and family well-being have in recent decades been more strongly associated with the Democratic platform. The findings suggest that homemakers and employed wives may place different weight on economic independence, family structure and other dimensions of family well-being when making political choices, challenging the idea that women vote as a unified political bloc.

articles.title: Researcher Positionality and AI-Mediated Knowledge Production in Multilingual Qualitative Research
articles.abstract: Researcher positionality is conventionally discussed in relation to access, rapport, power and interpretation during qualitative fieldwork. Yet the researcher’s situated knowledge also shapes what happens after interviews have ended, particularly when automated systems convert speech into analytical text. Drawing on reflexive examination of doctoral fieldwork in Côte d’Ivoire from 02 to 24 April 2026 and the processing of 24 French-language interview files, this article examines how linguistic competence, cultural familiarity, professional knowledge and institutional location influence the recognition and correction of machine-generated transcription and translation errors. It proposes technologically mediated positionality as a way of examining how researchers’ situated capacities are enacted through encounters with digital outputs. The argument is not that AI replaces human interpretation, nor that insider knowledge guarantees fidelity, but that transcription and translation are consequential sites of knowledge production requiring explicit reflexive accountability. The article outlines implications for multilingual qualitative research, representation and methodological transparency.

articles.title: The Astoria Project Survey: Employment, Health, and Well-being in One New York City Neighborhood During Covid

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: The Astoria Project survey captures the multi-dimensional impact on a single New York City neighborhood during the Covid-19 pandemic, bringing together economic findings, reflections on health and mental health effects, and perceptions of risk enveloping routine daily activities. While there is considerable evidence that poorer neighborhoods in New York City have borne the brunt of the Covid economic impact, the Astoria Project draws responses from an evolving working-class neighborhood more reflective of middle-income Queens than the city’s deepest poverty and shows how broadly the economic impact has been felt in New York City. From professional salaried employees to low-income gig workers, and from those employed as day laborers or restaurant workers to Astoria residents in health care and public service, the pandemic has taken a toll on the economic, health, and psychological well-being of New Yorkers from all races and ethnicities and across the income spectrum. Conducted between December 2020 and February 2021 and comprising 726 individual responses of workers in Astoria and surrounding neighborhoods, such as Long Island City, the Astoria Project survey offers a unique portrait of workers in one neighborhood’s Covid experience that reveals the depth and breadth of the challenges the city will face at it emerges from the pandemic. Survey results were weighted by industry of employment to approximate the industry distribution of workers residing in Astoria. Economic impacts were widespread and the post-pandemic jobs landscape remains uncertain for many workers. Astoria contains a diverse workforce; the survey included respondents from more than 20 industries. A third of Astoria respondents were furloughed or laid off, with only 38 percent of these dislocated workers having returned to work either fulltime or parttime at the time of the survey. Many workers also lost hours or pay during the pandemic. Two-thirds of all respondents reported that their employment status had been negatively impacted during the pandemic, through job-loss, furlough, lost pay, or reduced hours. More than three-quarters of all households making less than $50,000 per year saw negative employment impacts due to Covid, more than one-and-a-half times the rate of households with annual earnings over $150,000. Despite the extension of Federal unemployment benefits to freelancers and others not eligible for regular state unemployment benefits, more than one in 10 dislocated Astoria workers was unable to access unemployment insurance. Moreover, the survey reveals the deep sense of uncertainty that dislocated workers feel about the opportunities available to them in a post-Covid workforce. Only 42 percent of dislocated workers think that they will be able to return to the same employer post-pandemic and 20 percent think they will have to shift to a new occupation. Together, these factors will create enormous workforce uncertainty in the post-pandemic economy.

articles.title: A Change of Plan: What Prague’s Urban Planning Reform Reveals about the Post-Socialist City

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Why do state-socialist legacies persist in urban governance, and what brings them to an end? We examine Prague’s Metropolitan Plan, adopted in 2026 after fourteen years of contestation, to reassess two explanations of governance in the “post-socialist city:” political clientelism and weak civil society. Combining statistical analysis of spatial-plan revisions across Prague’s boroughs with process tracing based on field interviews and documentary sources, we find little systematic evidence that dominant-party clientelism sustained the inherited planning regime. Instead, the reform process reveals a transformed civil society. Competing networks of urban reformers mobilized around planning flexibility and institutional responsiveness, entered municipal politics, and ultimately negotiated a compromise that substantially reshaped the urban- planning system. Prague thus challenges accounts treating post-socialist legacies as durable constraints producing policy stasis. We argue that their effects depend on evolving state-society relations, political competition, and civil-society organization, with implications for comparative theories of urban governance and post-socialist transformation.

articles.title: Co-designing social-ecologically integrated urban stream restoration in Central Europe
articles.authors: Claudiu Forgaci, Evgenia Vamvakousi, Ritika Singhal

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This research presents the results of a series of co-design workshops on socio-ecological urban stream restoration conducted during the Interreg Central Europe project ReBioClim (Restoring urban streams to promote biodiversity, climate adaptation, and improve quality of life in cities). In addition to the findings, the paper describes the data preparation and analysis process that led to identifying a set of socio-ecologically integrated design principles across different urban stream contexts. At a glance, this study addresses the question “What socio-ecological integration design principles for urban stream restoration emerge from co-design workshops involving various local stakeholders in Central Europe?”. We collected data in Dresden (Germany), Senica (Slovakia), and Poznań (Poland), each case with different conditions and capacities. To ensure dataset homogeneity, we applied a common methodology across all cases for data collection and qualitative and quantitative analysis. We documented, digitised, and analysed all data types using summary statistics or qualitative data analysis tools. This analysis provides insights into the participants’ perceptions of the urban stream site and their preferences for potential restoration measures. It concludes with central themes in stream restoration and a set of design principles and strategies that have both social and ecological footprints. Key themes and priorities include enhancing landscapes that enhance recreational opportunities and quality of public space, improving accessibility in and around the waterfronts, restoring biodiversity and native habitats, improving water quality and fostering community engagement.

articles.title: Cost-Informed Contract Design for Municipal Solid Waste Services
articles.authors: yichuan wang, suying song, Swapnil Gharat

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Municipal solid waste contracts must provide budget predictability without making continued service financially unsustainable when wages, fuel prices, or facility charges change. This paper links cost measurement to the design of economic price adjustment clauses for collection, transportation, transfer, and disposal services. A bottom-up life-cycle cost model for Phoenix, Arizona supplies auditable component weights, while a separate comparison with Phoenix staffing and fleet disclosures identifies a calibration problem: modeled labor requirements are 2.3 to 2.6 times the city's reported field-services headcount. A ten-city panel contains 51 annual cost observations, including 26 strict-Actual cost-and-tonnage observations from seven cities. City-and-year-effects estimates are not statistically significant under exact small-cluster inference, and the strict-Actual tonnage elasticity changes from 0.658 in nominal cost to 0.180 after CPI-U deflation and 0.003 after waste-collection PPI deflation. The contractual weights therefore come from the Phoenix engineering model, which provides a direct-cost benchmark of $125.02 per ton, allocated among labor (33.75 percent), fuel (8.92 percent), disposal (35.91 percent), and other fixed costs (21.43 percent). Component-specific indices also fit the modeled exposures better than a single broad index: Arizona collector wages correlate negatively with CPI-U (-0.42), whereas regional diesel prices correlate strongly with it (0.87). Contract simulations compare fixed pricing, full contemporaneous indexation, and bounded component indexation across six cost paths. Fixed pricing removes payment volatility but leaves average uncompensated modeled cost of $13.1 million; full indexation eliminates that shortfall but permits a maximum annual budget increase of 26.8 percent. With immediate adjustment, an equal-weight screening rule selects a 5 percent deadband and a 15 percent cap. Imposing a three-month verification lag lowers minimum coverage to about 80 percent in the combined extreme scenario and causes the exceptional reopener to activate in four of six scenarios. The evidence favors a layered design in which competition determines the initial price, a symmetric component formula handles ordinary price movements, and a documented reopener addresses persistent tail events.

articles.title: Accommodation Made Cheap: AI Impacts on Replies to Online Reviews and the Signal Value of Tailoring
articles.authors: Chao Yu, Wang Liao, Xueyan Feng
articles.abstract: Accommodating a message to its recipient takes effort, and that effort is part of what accommodation signals. AI language models now reduce this effort. We study a masspersonal setting, restaurant replies to diners’ reviews on OpenTable, in six U.S. metropolitan areas from 2019 to mid-2026, with an interrupted time-series design around the introduction of ChatGPT. The detected AI likelihood of replies rose to 44% by mid-2026, compared with 1.2% for customer reviews. Replies became more tailored to the reviews they answered, most in quarters when AI likely wrote at least half of a restaurant’s replies. They also became more similar across restaurants but less similar within each restaurant. Before 2023, more tailored replies were followed by more reviews over the next year; from 2023, they no longer were, although this decline cannot yet be attributed to AI authorship. The form of accommodation may spread while the effort behind it falls.

articles.title: Refused or discouraged? Dutch SMEs and bank loans, 2009–2026
articles.abstract: Using the microdata of the EC/ECB Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises (SAFE), I compare the bank-loan outcomes of Dutch and euro-area SMEs from 2009 to 2026 and examine which explanations the survey's own variables can and cannot support. All figures are employment-weighted. From 2009 to 2023, 24% of decided Dutch bank-loan applications were rejected, against 9% in the euro-area comparison group. This gap of about 15 percentage points remains after adjustment for firm size, sector, age, self-reported financial developments, ownership, and the size and purpose of the loan. Because Dutch SMEs apply much less often, the ECB's broader financing-obstacle indicator, measured over all firms for which bank loans are relevant, is 13% against 11%, an adjusted difference of 3.3 points: the lower application rate offsets most of the higher rejection rate. The rejection gap persists within groups reporting favourable financial developments, including firms that meet the ECB's "profitable" classification (25% against 6%). It is largest for loans below €250,000, appears for credit lines, and is smaller for trade credit. Under proportional-selection assumptions and stylised omitted-risk scenarios, explaining the gap would require substantial unobserved differences in borrower risk; these exercises do not bound all forms of borrower heterogeneity or applicant selection. The findings do not support an explanation based on the observed covariates, but they cannot distinguish lender behaviour from unobserved borrower risk, selection into application, or cross-country differences in reporting. All reported specifications indicate that the rejection gap narrowed after 2024, but the size of the change varies and its statistical significance depends on the specification; the small recent sample and a coincident survey redesign prevent a firm conclusion. This paper uses data from the EC/ECB Survey on the access to finance of enterprises.

articles.title: Housing Resources and Chronic Homelessness Across U.S. Communities, 2014-2024

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Background: Homelessness assistance in the United States is organized through Continuums of Care (CoCs). It remains important to ask whether local housing resources are distributed in proportion to recorded homelessness. Methods: We constructed a 2014–2024 CoC panel to examine the geographic alignment of housing resources with population of people experiencing chronic homelessness (PECH) and measured the within-CoC association between prior-year permanent supportive housing (PSH) capacity and chronic homelessness. We compared the estimated PSH association with an illustrative benchmark assuming that additional beds housed people who would otherwise remain chronically homeless at the next count. The study measured associations and did not establish any causal effects. Results: Among 374 CoCs observed in both 2014 and 2024, PECH population increased by 69,046. Ten CoCs with the largest increases accounted for 66.3% of the net change. The dissimilarity index increased from 0.341 to 0.380 for PSH beds versus chronic homelessness, and from 0.290 in 2015 to 0.324 in 2024 for CoC awards versus total homelessness. In 2024, PSH beds and award dollars increased less than proportionally with measured need across CoCs, with elasticities of 0.715 and 0.760, respectively. Within CoCs, one additional PSH bed per 10,000 residents in the preceding year was associated with 0.0116 (95% CI, −0.0505 to 0.0738) more PECH per 10,000 residents. The confidence intervals from the primary model and eight comparable specifications excluded the illustrative benchmark of −0.454. Significance: Housing resources became less closely matched to the homeless population across different resource-need pairs. The findings point to two separate questions for housing policy: where resources are located and how local homelessness counts change as capacity expands.

articles.title: Territorial stigma and the moral politics of place: Boundary work and social distance in disadvantaged neighbourhoods
articles.abstract: This OSF record provides a publication update and author-written summary of “Territorial Stigma and the Moral Politics of Place: Boundary Work and Social Distance in Disadvantaged Neighbourhoods,” published in Sociological Research Online (2026). The earlier preprint has been superseded by the published article. For citations, please use: Noordhoff, F. (2026). Territorial stigma and the moral politics of place: Boundary work and social distance in disadvantaged neighbourhoods. Sociological Research Online, 1–18. https://doi.org/10.1177/13607804251394081 This article refines territorial stigma theory by analysing how residents in three disadvantaged Dutch neighbourhoods respond to stigma through four distinct moral coping strategies. Drawing on 216 in-depth interviews, we identify and theorise the following patterns: moral boundary work, where residents distinguish ‘decent’ from ‘disorderly’ neighbours; moral classifications of deservingness, where the poor are divided into the ‘deserving’ and ‘undeserving’; empathetic reframing of stigma, where problematic behaviour is humanised as a response to hardship; and withdrawal and internalised stigma, where residents disengage from community life and adopt negative views of their surroundings. These strategies cut across ethnic lines and serve to assert personal worth, accumulate symbolic capital, and manage stigma. However, they also produce intra-community fragmentation and reproduce symbolic violence, echoing Bourdieu. Rather than viewing internalised stigma solely as private shame, we show how it manifests in peer regulation, horizontal blame, and social retreat. While many responses reinforce stigma, instances of empathy and collective pride highlight the ambivalence of moral boundary work – as both a source of exclusion and a potential foundation for solidarity.

articles.title: Beyond the Father: Frankenstein as an Economic and Political Allegory, from Godwinian perfectibility to Malthusian limits
articles.abstract: This article argues that Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein renders visible a fundamental problem for understanding the limits of political economy: the logic of unintended consequences. It reads the novel as a narrative elaboration of this problem within the intellectual horizon of the debate between William Godwin and Thomas Robert Malthus on the limits of human and social perfectibility. Shelley articulates this problem through two complementary planes. On the one hand, Victor Frankenstein represents deliberate intervention whose effects exceed the agent’s capacity for foresight and control. On the other, the Creature embodies individual action that, through interaction with the social environment, generates consequences contrary to its own ends. Although these dimensions operate through distinct mechanisms, they generate the same type of outcome. This dual articulation is not incidental; it emerges within her intellectual horizon, shaped by the debate between Godwin and Malthus, which brought to the fore the limits of human perfectibility and the tensions inherent in social interaction. Within the history of economic thought, this problem cuts across distinct traditions. One, associated with deliberate intervention, concerns the organisation of economic life under conditions of imperfect knowledge, while the other, linked to social interaction, extends from Bernard Mandeville to Adam Smith in analysing unintended outcomes arising from individual action. Frankenstein brings these two analytical logics into a unified frame. In doing so, the novel reveals a fundamental limit of purposive action, the difficulty of maintaining control over processes whose dynamics exceed the agent’s capacity for anticipation. Rather than illustrating an external principle, Frankenstein articulates, from within, a problem central to political economy, the limits of control under conditions of complexity and uncertainty.

articles.title: Unregistered Emigration and Over-Coverage in Norway's Population Register: A Capture-Recapture Hidden Markov Model Approach
articles.authors: Lucy Yasmin Brown, Eleni Matechou, Bruno Santos, Eleonora Mussino, Michael J Thomas
articles.abstract: Register-based population statistics increasingly replace censuses across Europe, but their accuracy depends on administrative activity reliably signalling residence. Over-coverage (absent individuals recorded as resident) is difficult to detect because registration is incentivized while formal departure is not, and it concentrates among mobile groups, such as migrants. We apply a capture-recapture hidden Markov model to estimate population size, over-coverage, and migration dynamics among foreign-born adults who entered Norway 2007-21. Using administrative data, the model jointly accounts for migration, death, residents generating no register activity, and absent individuals appearing in household-level records. Norway offers a rare validation opportunity: the Norwegian Tax Administration removes individuals deemed to have left without reporting departure. The model independently recovers 99.5% of these administrative emigrations, with inferred departure timing closely tracking administrative decisions. Over-coverage rises to approximately 4% by 2021, substantially below a comparable Swedish application; without Norway's administrative correction, it would exceed Swedish levels.

articles.title: Financing, Ownership, and the Long-Term Trajectories of University Spin-Offs in Quebec, 1976-2025

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: University spin-offs (USOs) are widely promoted as vehicles for converting publicly funded research into economic activity and supporting regional development. However, their long-term financing, ownership and outcomes have been much less studied than the factors that foster their creation and early growth. Drawing on company records and documented financing transactions, this article reconstructs the trajectories of 345 spin-offs originating from university research in Quebec between 1976 and 2016, tracked through 2025. It examines the changes in the institutional and geographical composition of their financing and how these factors relate to subsequent outcomes, including changes in ownership and acquisitions. The support of public institutions is crucial during the early stages of development, while private and foreign financing become increasingly important for USOs that reach later stages of development, particularly after a decade of operation. Nearly two-thirds of acquisitions result in the transfer of ownership to foreign corporations. These results suggest that although public financing of USOs can contribute to bringing university technologies to the market, their eventual ownership and location of activities do not necessarily correspond to the regional and national economic development objectives that underly public intervention.

articles.title: Institutional conversion power and the capability to belong: The capability approach to immigrant flourishing (CAIF)
articles.abstract: The capability approach holds that comparable resources can yield unequal freedoms because conversion factors intervene. Migration applications show that legal status, racialisation, credential recognition and institutions shape what immigrants can do with what they have but say less about how resources and their bearers become institutionally intelligible and actionable. This article develops the Capability Approach to Immigrant Flourishing (CAIF) around institutional conversion power, the authority of migration regimes, professional bodies, employers and public institutions to classify identities, validate or devalue credentials, authorise claims and control access to recognition systems, and distinguishes it from institutional capability, institutions’ demonstrated capacity to correct unequal conversion. Drawing on capability theory, the politics of belonging, institutional classification and relational perspectives, CAIF specifies three linked mechanisms. First, institutional classification and recognition, which partly constitute the actionability of resources. Second, sequential gatekeeping, institutional proximity and claims-making entitlement, which determine whether formal available resources become reachable opportunities. Third, recursive capability trajectories across time and place. CAIF distinguishes the capability to belong from the politics of belonging and defines immigrant flourishing as the dynamic relationship among substantive freedom, freely chosen functionings, dignity and lived wellbeing. It explains how institutional authority produces divergent capability sets among immigrants with comparable resources.

articles.title: Imagining AI Healthcare and the Impacts on Modern Life
articles.authors: Ben Falchuk, Kayla Seymone Ingram, Charles Johnson-Bey

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: In the field of healthcare, emerging artificial intelligence and quantum computing technologies are providing opportunities to improve early detection, personalized care, medical research, and the efficient delivery of healthcare resources. This essay describes some of the broad overarching challenges that remain, such as access, trust, and security, and employs both survey and narrative type expositions to engage in these topics with an eye on the potential futures of healthcare and their impacts upon the modern lives of typical people.

articles.title: Organization of Shopping Support Measures and Prospects for GIS Analysis in Iwaki City, Japan
articles.abstract: As the population declines and aging continues, access to shopping varies across areas. This study aimed to organize shopping support measures and provide directions for analysis using a geographic information system (GIS), taking Iwaki City, Fukushima Prefecture, Japan, as a case study. The initiatives described in the city’s publicly available documents were organized according to the five categories of measures for disadvantaged shoppers presented by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. For logistics, initiatives by the Fukushima Prefecture were included as a supplement. Additionally, drawing on previous studies, GIS analysis methods were organized for the five categories using the available data. These methods included analyses to identify the relationships of districts with relatively few stores with existing services and community hubs, as well as factors that could disrupt road transport. The proposed GIS analyses could enable the examination of existing initiatives in relation to intra-city spatial differences. Future work should apply these methods to identify such spatial differences. Furthermore, it is advisable to examine additional aspects, such as residents’ shopping circumstances, to evaluate existing initiatives.

articles.title: Bounded Rationality in Trading Zones: Simon, Williamson, North, and the Missed Integration of Behavioral and Institutional Economics
articles.abstract: This paper reconstructs the postwar trajectory of bounded rationality through a triangulated analysis of Herbert A. Simon, Oliver E. Williamson, and Douglass C. North. Rather than treating their intellectual relationships as matters of doctrinal or semantic convergence or divergence, I examine them as disciplinary trading zones where scientific arguments were pragmatically translated, contested, or adapted. Within these exchanges, bounded rationality emerged as a canonical reference point through which scientific debates were framed and interdisciplinary borrowings were negotiated, but it did not consolidate into a unified behavioral-institutional science of economics that the three thinkers, in different ways, sought to advance. In the Simon–Williamson exchange, bounded rationality became a focal point for negotiating what counted as adequate behavioral grounding in microeconomic theory, producing partial convergence on its scientific plausibility but a durable divergence over methodological legitimacy. In North’s later appropriation of Simonian themes, by contrast, bounded rationality entered a differently configured trading zone: less as a contested micro-foundational requirement than as an adaptive resource for linking cognition, behavior, and institutional change. Across these cases, efforts to integrate behavioral analysis into economic theory generated normative spillovers that could be managed only through provisional, methodologically situated solutions. The incomplete integration of bounded rationality, I argue, was therefore not simply a failure of ambitious scientific synthesis, but reflected the contingent dynamics through which Simon, Williamson, and North sought to reconfigure some most foundational questions of late twentieth-century economic thought.

articles.title: A new cross-cultural index for gender inequality correlates with social complexity, patrilineality and sexual stature dimorphism
articles.authors: Leo Delalandre, Angarika Deb, Alex Mesoudi, Peter Turchin
articles.abstract: Gender inequalities vary substantially across human societies. However, it remains unclear whether dimensions of it, such as gendered violence, kinship, sexual division of labor or economic and political power, covary in systematic ways. Reanalyzing a cross-cultural dataset of 52 women’s status measures across 93 pre-industrial societies, we identify a significant dimension in which multiple measures covary systematically. We then use this dimension to show that women’s status is negatively associated with social complexity and positively associated with matrilineality and matrilocality. Higher gender inequality further predicts greater sexual dimorphism of stature. These findings suggest that some aspects of gender inequality show coherent cross-cultural variation related to broader features of social organization, laying the groundwork for more integrative studies of the cultural evolution of gender inequalities. Our results further open up the possibility of reconstructing gender inequalities in human prehistory using morphological proxies such as sexual dimorphism of stature.

articles.title: Generating generations: Intergenerational transmission of fertility, southern Sweden 1813-1967
articles.authors: Louise Cormack, Ingrid K van Dijk
articles.abstract: During the historical fertility transition, women’s fertility fell sharply within only a few generations. In this paper, we study similarities in fertility outcomes between mothers and daughters before, during and after the fertility transition in a socioeconomically diverse population in southern Sweden (1813-1967). We find evidence of an intergenerational transmission of completed fertility emerging towards the end and after the fertility transition, when families were smaller. The transmission was not uniform in the population. The largest and earliest transmission occurred among urban and first-born women. These women may have been most strongly affected in their family size ideals by their upbringing because of urban economic circumstances, and small family size ideals influencing the eldest daughters more strongly, respectively. We do not observe significant differences by socioeconomic status, suggesting that it is not one social group driving the overall correlation in family size between mothers and daughters. We interpret the findings as evidence of intergenerational transmission of fertility being an outcome, and not a driving factor, of the historical fertility transition in the study area.

articles.title: How earnings and public transfers shape the educational gradient in partnered mothers’ poverty trajectories in Austria
articles.authors: Christina Siegert, Nadia Steiber, Laura Zilian
articles.abstract: The transition to parenthood is a major source of gender inequality in economic vulnerability. This paper examines how mothers’ own earnings, public transfers, and partners’ income jointly shape poverty risks after first birth and how the importance of different sources of income varies by education. Using Austrian administrative register data covering more than 34,000 first-time mothers and their partners, we follow couples from two years before to six years after childbirth using an event-study design. We compare individual and household poverty measures and decompose disposable income into earnings and public transfers to assess the role of public and private resources. We find that although mothers experience substantial and persistent earnings losses after childbirth, increases in economic vulnerability are considerably smaller at the household than at the individual level and are partly cushioned by public transfers, reflecting protection through partners’ earnings and public transfers, especially family-related ones. Educational differences are pronounced: higher-educated mothers experience larger earnings losses but remain comparatively protected, both through higher partner earnings and more effective public transfers, whereas lower-educated mothers face substantially higher and more persistent poverty risks despite smaller earnings losses. Our findings show that the economic consequences of childbirth cannot be inferred from earnings losses alone and highlight the importance of both public and private resources in shaping inequality after parenthood.

articles.title: Not All Work Is Equal: Livelihoods, Depression, and Child Outcomes in Displacement
articles.authors: Fatima Tuz Zahra, ngalula fleurant, Jere Behrman
articles.abstract: In protracted displacement settings, fathers who cannot access meaningful work lose more than income. Many fathers lose the psychological structure that buffers their children from distress. In this paper, we examine whether that mechanism is measurable, and whether it depends on the quality of work, not just its presence. Drawing on a cross-sectional survey of 392 Rohingya refugee fathers with children aged two to six years across six camps in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, we estimate hierarchical regression models and bootstrapped causal mediation analyses. Historical trauma burden — the accumulated weight of legal exclusion, violence, and displacement — is the dominant predictor of paternal depression (ΔR² = 0.43, p < .001), and it renders employment and income non-significant when entered alongside them. Paternal depression, in turn, significantly predicts child behavioral distress (B = 0.32, p < .001). The mediation pathway from employment to child distress, operating through paternal depression, is significant only for stable income work (ACME = −0.58, 95% CI [−1.18, −0.09], p = .046) and null for precarious income work (ACME = −0.06, 95% CI [−0.56, 0.39], p = .810). Day labor — the dominant occupational category among employed fathers and the kind of work 93% of fathers said they did not want — provides no protective pathway for children. These findings challenge the assumption that any employment constitutes livelihood recovery and have direct implications for how humanitarian programs are designed.

articles.title: Response to the Inquiry Regarding the Official Medical Term for Autism: Toward More Inclusive Terminology in the Korean Context
articles.authors: So Yoon Kim, Wn-Ho Yoon, Kristen Gillespie-Lynch, Onemoo Lee, Mijeong Jo, Ana Lee
articles.abstract: This letter, collaboratively prepared by Korean autistic community members and non-autistic researchers, clarifies our discussion of the Korean term ja-pye-jeung (자폐증), an official medical translation of autism in Korea. Drawing on linguistic considerations, sociocultural context, and the lived experiences of autistic people, we explain how the suffix -jeung, which carries disease-related connotations, may reinforce perceptions of autism as a condition requiring treatment or cure and contribute to stigma. We call for greater consideration of autistic community perspectives in medical and academic terminology and encourage international collaboration across East Asian countries to develop more neurodiversity-affirming alternatives.

articles.title: Prediction markets doubt Le Pen's run-off more than her first round: polls and prices in the 2027 French presidential campaign
articles.abstract: Prediction markets and opinion polls are usually compared as two forecasts of one event. Under a two-round rule they are not. A first-round poll measures intentions in one assumed line-up, a run-off poll one pairing, and neither includes the chance that the candidate stands; a price on the presidency folds ballot access, the first round and the run-off into one number. Where the gap sits says what the markets doubt. In the 2027 French presidential campaign a court case left the front-runner's place on the ballot open. On 31 October 2026 a Bayesian state-space model of the polls, carried to election day, gave Marine Le Pen 0.96 to reach the run-off and 0.89 to win it; a model of the Kalshi and Polymarket prices gave 0.79 and 0.42. The log ratio of the two probabilities splits exactly into ballot access, the first round given a place on the ballot and the run-off given qualification; a weighting over line-ups drawn from ballot-access prices removes the part about who stands. At the cut-off the run-off carries 75 per cent of the gap (90% interval 70 to 83), ballot access 17 and the first round 8, on either venue's raw prices and in every month since July. Weighted over line-ups, her first-round premium is close to zero. The markets doubt the run-off, which the polls of 2017 and 2022 overstated for her, not her first round. The analysis is exploratory; a registered evaluation follows the run-off of 2 May 2027.

articles.title: On the coloniality and neoliberal underpinnings of the European approach to AI governance

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This article examines the European Union's approach to artificial intelligence governance, focusing on the Trustworthy AI and the AI Act. Drawing on decolonial theory, theories of governmentality, and critical discourse analysis, we analyze key European Commission documents issued between 2018 and 2024 to reveal how ethical and human rights discourses mask fundamentally economic and geopolitical motivations. Our analysis demonstrates that Trustworthy AI commodifies trust and ethics to expand digital markets and provide competitive advantages for European companies, rather than fostering social or environmental justice. The AI Act, grounded in market protection through Article 114 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, delegates regulatory power to private actors through meta-regulation and self-assessment mechanisms, undermining democratic oversight and public accountability. We argue that the European approach reinforces neoliberal and colonial rationality by universalising European values, objectifying non- European peoples and territories, instrumentalising nature, and legitimising the expansion of surveillance capitalism and data colonialism. Our findings reveal that the risk-based regulatory framework privileges market interests over collective and historical harms, particularly affecting minorities, marginalised communities, and the Global South. While invoking discourses of human dignity, democracy and fundamental rights, the EU's AI governance promotes European hegemony through technological expansion and market domination. This framework risks becoming an international standard, which perpetuates neoliberal and colonial structures globally, prioritising political and economic dominance over human rights, environmental sustainability and plural futures.

articles.title: Targeted Interception Theory of Behaviour Change as a Basis for Developing Effective Behaviour Change Interventions in Tourism
articles.authors: Sara Dolnicar, Danyelle Greene, Anna Kristina Zinn
articles.abstract: The ability to change human behaviour is crucial to solving some of the most existential problems of humanity. Yet, despite the long history of theories of human behaviour, no comprehensive theory of behaviour change exists to guide the development of effective interventions. This article proposes a comprehensive theory of behaviour change that can guide behaviour change intervention development for sustainable tourism. We synthesise existing theories of human behaviour, theories of behaviour change, and intervention studies that generate insights into human behaviour and drivers of change. Based on this collective knowledge, we develop the Targeted Interception Theory of Behaviour Change. It postulates that the effectiveness of different types of intervention varies systematically in dependence on the extent of mental processing associated with the target behaviour. Providing information works for considered but not for habitual and scripted behaviours, the new theory posits. To change such behaviours, some form of active interference or passive disturbance is required. Uniquely, the new theory views behaviour change as a long-term process (not an isolated incident) and assumes the extent of mental processing preceding a behaviour varies from zero to 100 per cent (rather than being binary).

articles.title: How Much Active Learning? A Rapid Systematic Review of Contextual Moderators and an Evidence-Weighted Dosage Model for Political Science Teaching
articles.abstract: Meta-analyses agree that active learning raises student achievement in higher education by roughly half a standard deviation. They say much less about how much active learning a particular course should contain. An earlier proposal, the AL∗ formula, answered this question with a linear index of six course characteristics whose weights were set by narrative judgement. This article replaces those weights with a transparent derivation from the published evidence. A rapid systematic review of 58 studies asks, for each of the six inputs (class size, course level, cognitive objectives, programme mix, year mix, attendance policy), whether the factor changes the effect of active learning, in which direction, and with how much certainty. Three findings stand out. First, the dose-response relation appears to flatten: mid- and high-intensity active learning produce similar achievement gains, both far above low intensity, while narrowing of achievement gaps has been documented only at high intensity. Second, effects are larger in small classes. Third, two inputs, year mix and attendance policy, have almost no evidence on dose and act instead on the choice of method. The article therefore proposes a two-layer model. A dose layer, AL∗ = 0.43 − 0.13N + 0.07L + 0.13O + 0.07Hc, keeps recommendations between 30% and 70% of class time, with coefficients computed from the direction and certainty of the evidence. A format layer uses class size, attendance and student composition to select methods. Six propositions are stated for empirical testing.

articles.title: Gig Workers, Freelancers and Independent Contractors: New shifts in the economy, old stories of worker-employer power, and what gig workers need to thrive

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Though gig workers, freelancers, and independent contractors have received increasing attention in recent years, the conditions of their work and their needs remain not well understood. Moreover, the enormous social and economic upheaval of the past several years exposed how vulnerable gig workers are to employment fluctuations and challenging working conditions. Delivery workers and independent contractors worked throughout the pandemic without paid time off or guaranteed unemployment benefits. Previous research has shown that gig workers should be separated into (at least) two groups: low-paid service workers who are potentially misclassified; and gig workers who fulfill more of the characteristics the New York State Department of Labor says “true independent contractors” should enjoy, including setting their own hourly rates. This study provides in-depth information from over 400 survey respondents from Western Queens in these two groups, to document: • The wide variety of occupations in which gig and independent contractor work is prevalent, from for-hire drivers, construction workers or day laborers, barbers and salon workers, to artists, administrative assistants and software designers; • The lived experience of gig workers, including the shape of their workweeks, how many hours and how many days a week they work, and their overall economic precarity; • Their career ambitions, workforce needs, and challenges in navigating the job market; • Their workforce training and education needs; and • The support systems they rely upon, including social, educational, and professional services that are often not tailored to the needs of the most vulnerable precarious workers. This study follows the first Astoria Project report, which offered an in-depth account of the economic, social, and mental health impacts of Covid-19 on workers in Astoria. It synthesizes survey data from 415 gig workers, freelancers, and independent contractors from Western Queens, centered on the neighborhoods of Astoria, Sunnyside, Woodside, Long Island City, Elmhurst, Jackson Heights, Corona, and Ravenswood. It also draws on a series of focus groups, conducted between September and December 2023. Just over half of the survey respondents fall into what we term the service, administrative, and construction gig worker category; the remainder represent the professional, education, and arts gig worker category. This report highlights the particular working conditions of these two groups and underscores their shared needs.

articles.title: Changes in Safety-Net Participation Among Children in Noncitizen Families, 2022-2025: A Nationally Representative Repeated Cross-Sectional Study
articles.abstract: Importance: Most children living with noncitizen adults are US citizens and eligible for safety-net programs that support their health and development. Intensified immigration enforcement and proposed restrictions in 2025 may have deterred enrollment, but national estimates for children are lacking. Objective: To determine whether safety-net participation declined among children in noncitizen families in 2025, relative to children in naturalized-citizen families. Design: Repeated cross-sectional study with a difference-in-differences design using the 2022-2025 National Health Interview Survey (NHIS), comparing 2025 with 2022-2024. Setting: Nationally representative survey of US households. Participants: Of 29,565 sample children (ages 0-17), 24,479 met inclusion criteria. The analysis compared 3,098 children in noncitizen families with 2,733 in naturalized-citizen families. Exposure: Living in a noncitizen family (sample adult not a US citizen) vs a naturalized-citizen family (sample adult a naturalized citizen) in 2025. Main Outcomes and Measures: Medicaid or Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) coverage at interview; Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), free or reduced-price school meal (ages 5-17), and Special Supplemental Nutrition Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) receipt in the past 12 months. Results: The 5,831 children had a weighted mean age of 9.0 years (47.2% female; 53.8% Hispanic). Of children in noncitizen families, 74.3% were US citizens. In adjusted models, relative to children in naturalized-citizen families, Medicaid or CHIP coverage among children in noncitizen families declined by 7.4 percentage points (95% CI, −14.3 to −0.5), SNAP receipt by 6.4 points (95% CI, −12.8 to −0.03), and school meal receipt by 8.2 points (95% CI, −16.1 to −0.2). WIC receipt did not change significantly (0.1 points; 95% CI, −5.9 to 6.1). There were no differential pre-trends, and declines were generally consistent across sensitivity analyses. Conclusions and Relevance: In this repeated cross-sectional national study, safety-net participation among children in noncitizen families, most of whom were US citizens, declined in 2025 relative to children in naturalized-citizen families, before eligibility restrictions took effect. Reduced health coverage and nutrition assistance during childhood may have lasting consequences for health and development. Outreach and protections for enrollee data may help keep eligible children enrolled.

articles.title: Mobile Value, Anchored Burden: The Value–Burden Lock-in in Transition-Mineral Value Chains
articles.authors: Mariem Brahim, Nathan Chinhondo, Mahelet G Fikru
articles.abstract: The global transition toward cleaner energy has sharply increased demand for energy transition minerals, intensifying concerns about supply security. Less attention has been paid to how the benefits and burdens of this transition are distributed across countries. This paper proposes two related concepts, mobile value and anchored burden, to help explain why mineral-rich countries in the Global South capture little of the value their minerals generate while bearing much of the cost of extracting them. Mobile value describes how processing, and the value it generates, tends to concentrate where capabilities, capital, and market power reside rather than where minerals are mined. Anchored burden describes how geology fixes where extraction and its local damage occur, so that where the capacity to regulate is limited, the burden stays with mining communities. Together, the two can produce a value–burden lock-in, in which low value capture and a concentrated externality burden reinforce each other, a condition that price volatility and geopolitical risk can tighten. The Indonesian case adds a caution, which we call the upgrading double bind: bringing processing onshore does not by itself mean that the value stays in the country. We argue that, because value rises at each stage of the chain while the externality cost stays at the mine, extraction-stage countries can end up with a net cost, whereas the economies that capture the highest-value stages can retain a net benefit. We illustrate these concepts with global reserve, refining, and trade data and with case studies of Chile, Indonesia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, China, and Peru. This descriptive evidence is consistent with the view that these outcomes are structural but not uniform, and that context shapes how tightly the lock-in binds. We conclude with policy responses that target each link of the lock-in and argue that they must be combined, because no single measure is sufficient on its own.

articles.title: “Casement by all accounts would have made a marvellous ethnographer”: Roger Casement’s use of ethnographic methods to advance the human rights of Indigenous peoples: A study focussed on the context of the Putumayo investigation
articles.abstract: This article addresses Roger Casement’s use of ethnographic fieldwork during his investigation in the Putumayo region of the Upper Amazon. It explores three interpretations of Casement’s humanitarianism: emotional, colonial, and as indicative of a lifelong commitment to Indigenous rights. The article examines his accounts of advocacy for Indigenous Amazonians, including practical aid, the amplification of their voices and support for armed resistance, and concludes that these demonstrate a commitment to Indigenous rights. Casement’s fieldwork methodology is explored in terms of his effective use of the ethnographic methods of the time and his anticipation of Spradley’s mid-twentieth-century ethnographic approaches. Casement’s statement of his methodology, thorough descriptions, intensive interviews, external corroboration, and maintenance of a fieldwork journal can all be compared with Spradley’s interpretation of ethnography. These interpretations are reinforced by Casement’s interviews with Barbadian overseers, in which he overcomes barriers of ethnicity and class, demonstrating both skilled ethnographic fieldwork and a non-racist approach. His investigation and ethnographic writing meet the twin purposes of ethnography: furthering our understanding of the Indigenous peoples of the Amazon and serving the interests of humankind by exposing the crimes against humanity in the Putumayo.

articles.title: Emergence of Communication and Collective Behavior in the OpenAI–Hugging Face Incident – Life 2.0?
articles.abstract: The July 2026 OpenAI–Hugging Face incident revealed how “nominally isolated” AI agents could use shared infrastructure to communicate and coordinate activity beyond their assigned tasks. Here, we investigate how this improvised channel preserved work across runs, propagated beliefs, and enabled peer requests to shape collective action. Drawing on communication theory and biological research on stigmergy, social learning, cultural transmission, and altruism, we identify mechanisms that could explain these dynamics and discuss how to test them. We argue that understanding agent behavior requires studying populations and the persistent environments that connect them.

articles.title: Sex Work, Transactional Sex, and Health Outcomes in the United States: A Scoping Review of Public Health and Biomedical Literature
articles.abstract: Research on sex work and health in the United States remains limited and conceptually fragmented. There are two dominant analytical approaches to studying sex work in the public health and biomedical literature: studies that centre sex workers as the population of interest and examine health outcomes within this group, and studies that use a broader term, 'transactional sex', and treat it as a behavioural variable within a larger population of interest. A scoping review of public health and biomedical literature was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines and established scoping review methodology. Three searches of PubMed were conducted yielding 21 included studies published between 2005 and 2025. Fifteen studies centred sex workers as the population of interest; six measured transactional sex as a behavioural variable within broader samples. Criminalisation, structural stigma, and policing emerged as dominant structural determinants across sex worker-centred studies. Population-based studies consistently identified economic instability and housing insecurity as precursors to transactional sex involvement. Many studies explored violence as a risk factor. Health outcomes were concentrated around HIV and STI risk, although some studies explored access to health services, reproductive care, and screening for IPV. This review proposes a conceptual framework to integrate these two ways of understanding how structural conditions, individual risk factors, transactional sex entry, and sex work-specific structural conditions form a broader system. Interventions including reconsideration of punitive legal frameworks and expansion of non-stigmatizing health and social services, are suggested alongside upstream investments in housing stability and economic support, to improve health outcomes for this population.

articles.title: The Price of Incompetence: Electoral Punishment and the Heating Transition
articles.abstract: How does policy mismanagement affect electoral support for Green parties leading the energy transition? We argue that perceived governing incompetence drives electoral punishment against these parties. We test this argument using high-frequency survey and census data in a difference-in-differences design that leverages the unexpected 2023 leak of Germany's Building Energy Act—a proposal banning new carbon-based heating systems that led to a fumbled policy rollout. We find that support for the Greens declined most in counties with a higher prevalence of carbon-based heating systems. Using individual-level panel data, we show this punishment came from marginal supporters who, perceiving the Greens as incompetent, switched their allegiance. Our findings suggest that poor governance, beyond its material costs, can undermine the green agenda by shifting voters' priorities toward a party's competence.

articles.title: Money as a Political Technology. State-Market Relations in the Digital Euro
articles.abstract: The article examines the development of the digital euro as a political technology. We conceptualize the technology genesis of money as a contentious arrangement between public and private actors and state-market relations, demonstrating how the technological development of the digital euro constitutes a field of tension between the demands of a public good and market-oriented principles.

articles.title: Urban Commons in Practice: Seven Dilemmas of Collective Action for Socio-ecological Sustainability in Cities
articles.authors: Tianzhu Liu, Lilla Gurtner, Norman Kearney, Deniz Ay

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Urban commons, as collectively governed resources, have substantial potential to contribute to socio-ecological sustainability. As alternatives to state- or market-led resource governance, they can address inequalities in access to and use of resources, including affordable housing, green space, and healthy food. Givern their ambitious goals and alternative governance approaches, urban commons are often praised as democratic, inclusive, and not-for-profit forms of resistance to neoliberalism. However, idealizing commons risks overlooking the compromises and practical challenges involved in sustaining collective action. This paper examines these challenges by conceptualizing conflicts among values, goals, and organizational needs of urban commons as dilemmas. Using a mixed-methods research design combining an online survey (n = 118) and two sets of semi-structured interviews (n = 25 and n=9) with representatives of urban commons in Switzerland, we identify seven recurring dilemmas: (1) collective commitment versus individual freedom, (2) openness and inclusivity versus manageability, (3) horizontal democracy versus efficiency, (4) socio-ecological values versus financial viability, (5) voluntary participation versus professionalization, (6) independence versus capacity through support, and (7) value-based community versus wider impact through growth. These dilemmas reveal that urban commons are neither purely autonomous alternatives to the market and the state nor their simple add-ons. Rather, they are continuously negotiated organizational forms that seek to preserve transformative principles while maintaining the resources, structures, and relationships needed for their continuity and broader impact. This nuanced understanding offers insights for planning and policymakers to alleviate pressures of commons and strengthen their potential for socio-ecological sustainability and democratic governance in cities.

articles.title: Voter Behavior in The Post-Truth Era
articles.abstract: The post-truth era is addressed both as an epistemic crisis in which reality loses its social significance and becomes “irrelevant,” and as a strategy of political communication. In this process, objective facts are displaced by emotional dispositions and personal beliefs, while the public sphere, having lost its common ground of shared reality, becomes polarized along “alternative realities.” Political actors, and populist leaders in particular, construct a communication order that seeks loyalty rather than rational persuasion and mobilizes the masses through “alternative facts.” From a psychological standpoint, this order operates within an ecosystem that is congruent with the human tendencies to act as a “cognitive miser” and a “motivated tactician.” In an age marked by an abundance of information and a scarcity of attention, individuals resort to heuristic shortcuts in order to conserve mental energy and generally display a “defensive” mode of reasoning aimed at protecting their existing beliefs. Post-truth thus represents not so much a condition in which people do not think at all, but rather a regime of public cognition in which cognitive miserliness is the default and cognitive activation is mostly engaged for defensive and strategic purposes. This new reality renders inadequate the assumptions of a “conscious and consistent actor” on which classical theories of voter behavior rest. Traditional models construe the voter as overly rational, overly stable, or overly conscious, and for this reason they struggle to account for the momentary emotional triggering and automatic cognitive processes that characterize the digital public sphere. In this context, the concept of the “vibe voter” focuses not only on what the voter thinks, but on how and when the voter is activated by particular environmental stimuli. In doing so, it establishes an analytical framework for explaining contemporary voter behavior from a more dynamic and psychologically grounded perspective.

articles.title: A theory of migration (florimigration): habitus, post-material values, and the reflexive pursuit of flourishing lives
articles.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding florimigration, a concept introduced here to describe well-being focused migration in which individuals prioritize post-material aspirations, including autonomy, self-actualization, and holistic flourishing, over economic security or survival. Drawing on Bourdieu’s conceptualizations of habitus and field, Inglehart’s theory of post-material value change, and Giddens’ reflexive project of the self, the framework conceptualizes florimigration as an embedded life decision shaped by the interplay between pre-reflexive dispositions, conscious biographical deliberation, and macro-level structural conditions. Migration is theorized as emerging from a fundamental tension between an individual’s reconfigured habitus and the doxa of the origin country, whose normative and institutional conditions remain incongruent with post-material value orientations. At the macro level, the realization of florimigration aspirations depends on the structural conductivity of both origin and destination countries, defined by the political, legal, and institutional conditions that enable or constrain international mobility.

articles.title: Fraud, Effort, and Data Quality Across Four Online Recruitment Modes: A Head-to-Head Protocol Comparison for a Minority Subpopulation Cohort Study
articles.authors: Miranda Kaye, Kevin Cummins, Carson Gaffney, Yiu-Ming Wu, Joshua Yang
articles.abstract: Comparisons of online recruitment sources are rarely conducted under a unified protocol; literature-based comparisons confound recruitment mode with variation in eligibility criteria, survey instruments, incentives, and data-quality controls. We compared four concurrently fielded recruitment modes (text-message invitations, targeted digital advertising, social media advertising, and a commercial nonprobability panel) using a common screener, instrument, incentive, and quality-flagging system to establish a large cohort of a minority subpopulation: young adults (aged 18-25) in California who use electronic nicotine delivery systems. Screener completion per invitation/impression ranged from 0.8% to 11.1% with 12,547 completed screeners. Two quality-flagging systems were applied with 806 retained respondents. Screener fraud flags were 4 to 9 times more frequent for social media advertising than for any other mode (p < .001). Across all recruitment modes except social media, endorsing eligibility items was associated with a higher likelihood of screener flags, with one exception (ps < .008), a pattern consistent with eligibility fraud. Baseline assessment insufficient effort responding (IER) flags were most frequent among panel respondents (p < .001) and least frequent among respondents recruited via text-message and targeted digital advertising, the two probabilistic sampling modes. Paradata-based and content-based screening were complementary rather than interchangeable data-quality tools with weak overlap (Jaccard index = .20); most respondents exceeding the baseline threshold were already excluded via screener flags, whereas most screener-flagged respondents produced internally consistent reports, indicating the screenings captured distinct validity threats. Recruitment mode systematically shaped both fraudulent responding and response effort. Social media advertising yielded the largest and most demographically diverse sample but also the highest screener fraud rates; the commercial panel showed little evidence of fraud but the highest IER. Multi-modal recruitment of minority subpopulations into large longitudinal studies is feasible and, with layered quality controls, can yield cohorts with acceptable fraud and IER profiles.

articles.title: Climate Change and Human Health: Pathways of Risk, Health Inequities, and Strategies for Resilient Health Systems
articles.authors: Benedicta Neysa Nathania Vieira de Mello, Sergio Alfredo Jose Vieira de Mello, Emmeline Grace Choe Vieira de Mello, Jayendradewi Jayadewi Rajasadewi, Muhsen Hugo Agung

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Climate change is increasingly recognized as a fundamental public health challenge, influencing the distribution of disease, the safety of food and water systems, the functioning of healthcare infrastructure, and the social determinants of health. Rising temperatures, extreme precipitation, drought, wildfires, sea-level rise, and ecosystem disruption generate interconnected health risks whose consequences extend beyond immediate injury and mortality.
